text: [REDACTED_ORIGINAL_PASSAGE]Methods Records of patients with stage IV melanoma who received ICI therapy at Moffitt between 01/2010-03/2020 were reviewed. Descriptive and multivariate analyses conducted using R (Version 4.3.0).3 Kaplan-Meier curves were used to calculate time to treatment discontinuation (TTD), as a surrogate for PFS, and OS. Results This cohort consisted of 876 patients with a median age of 67 years (range 17–93) and male predominance (68%). Fifty percent received anti-PD1 monotherapy, 34% anti-CTLA4 monotherapy, and 16% combination anti-PD1 and anti-CTLA4 as first line ICI. Sixty-three percent of patients had antibiotic exposure between six before and after ICI with varied timing of antibiotic exposure in relationship to ICI. Average TTD was 5.8 months versus 6.0 months in the exposed versus non-exposed groups respectively. Antibiotic exposure at any time was not associated with shorter TTD (hazard ratio [HR] = 1.01; 95% CI 0.85–1.20) or OS (HR = 0.96; 95% CI 0.76–1.22). Timing of antibiotic in relation to ICI also did not impact TTD or OS. Impact of exposure to specific antibiotics of interest including vancomycin, metronidazole, and piperacillin-tazobactam (pip-tazo) was investigated. Metronidazole and pip-tazo exposure had no significant impact on TTD nor OS. Vancomycin exposure was associated with a decreased TTD (HR = 1.26; 95% CI 1.03–1.53) and worse OS (HR = 1.79; 95% CI 1.40–2.29). Conclusions In this large cohort of patients with advanced melanoma receiving ICI, there was no significant difference in TTD or OS between those exposed versus not exposed to antibiotics. TTD and OS were not impacted by timing of antibiotic. This differs from earlier data but more recent studies have been mixed.4 Vancomycin had a significant negative impact on TTD and OS whereas antibiotics with more gastrointestinal coverage such as metronidazole and pip-tazo did not. Further investigation is needed to define the specific characteristics of antibiotic exposure that impact ICI therapy and better understand mechanistic drivers. Ethics Approval This study was approved by institutional review board of Moffitt Cancer Center, Study ID: MCC 20496. All required consents were acquired prior to data collection.
